description: Largest contiguous land empire in history (1206–1368) founded by Genghis Khan; its military innovations, combined arms tactics, siege engineering, psychological warfare, conquered territory from Korea to Poland; while destructive, its Pax Mongolica created the conditions for the first sustained Eurasian trade network, and its successor states shaped Persian, Chinese, Russian, and Turkish civilisations profoundly.

temporal.notes: Founded by Genghis Khan 1206; fragmented into four khanates; Yuan dynasty falls 1368

lifecycle_phases.description: Genghis Khan unites Mongol tribes; conquers northern China, Khwarezmian Empire, and Kievan Rus
Sons and grandsons complete conquest of China, Persia, Baghdad (1258), and invade Poland and Hungary
Empire splits into four khanates: Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, Chagatai Khanate, Yuan Dynasty; lose cohesion

rise_factors.description: Mongol cavalry combined extreme mobility with coordinated tactics, devastating settled armies across Eurasia
Decimal organization (arbans, jaghuns, mingghans, tumens), meritocratic promotion, and sophisticated siege warfare technology
Exploited political fragmentation of Jin China, Kievan Rus, and Islamic world to divide and conquer

Genghis Khan reorganized the Mongol army on decimal units (arban 10, zuun 100, myangan 1000, tumen 10,000) cutting across tribal lines. This disrupted inter-tribal conflict and created a professional military hierarchy loyal to the Khan rather than tribal chiefs.

The Yasa (Great Law) codified Mongol customary law, creating uniform legal standards across conquered territories. Its pragmatic tolerance, protecting merchants, exempting clergy, guaranteeing messenger safety, made Mongol governance predictable and commerce-friendly.

At its height, the Mongol Empire created the largest free trade zone in history: the Pax Mongolica (c.1250–1350) allowed merchants to travel from China to Europe under Mongol protection, carrying silk, spices, and plague-carrying rats.

Mongol commanders systematically used terror as strategic policy: cities that surrendered received lenient treatment; those that resisted were massacred to the last inhabitant. This made subsequent cities far more likely to surrender, dramatically reducing siege costs.

decline_factors.description: No clear succession mechanism; civil wars between Genghis Khan's descendants led to permanent fragmentation
Vast overextension across Eurasia made integrated governance impossible; regional khanates became independent

Mongol succession required a kurultai (assembly of princes) to elect the next Khan. This consensus requirement became unworkable as the empire grew: regional khans refused to attend, recognized different successors, and succession wars became endemic after Möngke Khan's death (1259).

The Black Death originated in Mongol-controlled Central Asia (c.1346) and spread along Mongol-maintained trade routes. The devastation reduced Mongol population across Eurasia and disrupted the administrative networks that held the empire together.
